title: Who sweeps a room
hookLine: Herbert's The Elixir: sweeping a room for God makes it fine
carry: makes that and the action fine
tomorrow: a cook kept forgetting God all day. what did he do about it?

lines: A STONE THAT TURNS THINGS TO GOLD.
cards: The scrape of a broom. Grit under your shoes in the kitchen. A dish rack that refills the second you empty it.
Chores are the part of the day nobody posts. So what could turn sweeping a dusty floor into gold?
George Herbert has an answer, and he put it in a poem called The Elixir, after the stone that old stories said could turn plain metal into gold. His stone isn't in a lab. It's a short phrase.

teach.b: The poem opens as a request: "Teach me, my God and King, In all things thee to see, And what I do in any thing, To do it as for thee." As for thee. That's the phrase.
Then Herbert walks into the plainest room in the house.
"A servant with this clause Makes drudgery divine: Who sweeps a room, as for thy laws, Makes that and th' action fine." Look at what changes. Not the broom.
Not the dust. Not the room. The reason.

teach.h: THE ROOM AND THE ACTION, FINE.
teach.b: Same strokes, done for someone, and Herbert says two things become fine: the room, and the act of sweeping it. Then he names his secret: "This is the well-known stone That turneth all to gold."
He's leaning on Paul, who told the Colossians: "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." There's a picture in the poem for how this works, too.
You can look at a window and stop at the glass, smudges and all.

teach.h: MAKES THAT AND THE ACTION FINE.
teach.b: Or you can look through it, and the poem says then the heavens come into view. Sweeping is the glass. One to tell a friend: Herbert's word for drudgery and his word for divine sit side by side in one line.

how: Herbert's The Elixir is sung as the hymn 'Teach me, my God and King' in some churches; many Christians draw on Colossians 3:23 to treat ordinary work as done for God.

games.q: what does “who sweeps a room” mean?
o: Herbert's picture of a chore done as for God, and made fine
an old church job: the caretaker who cleaned the chapel
a proverb that a clean house shows a clean soul

games.q: inside The Elixir — tap the pairs.
p: makes that and th' action fine
look through it and see the heavens

s: to make a chore holy, you have to pray out loud while doing it
in Herbert's poem nothing is added to the sweeping. it's done as for thee, and that's the change.
in the poem, both the room and the act of sweeping become fine
makes that and th' action fine: the room, and the doing of it.
Herbert's 'well-known stone' is a real stone from the Bible
it's the stone of old stories that turns metal to gold. his stone is a phrase: as for thee.

games.q: your little brother says chores are just punishment and asks why your mom hums while she mops. what does Herbert's poem say could change a chore?
o: the reason: doing it as for someone.
doing it perfectly, with no dust left.
doing it fast enough to get it over with.
games.why: same broom, same dust. Herbert says doing it 'as for thee' makes the room and the action fine.

practice: Take a broom, or a cloth if there's no broom nearby, and clean one small patch: a step, a counter, a corner. Go slowly, one stroke on each out-breath, and listen to the bristles.
Do it as for someone: for God if you pray, for the next person who walks there if you don't.

wordCard.voice: Who sweeps a room. Herbert's plainest chore, done as for thee, and turned to gold without changing a single stroke.

orig.note: Greek: as to the Lord. Paul's phrase in Colossians 3:23, behind Herbert's 'as for thee'.

carryVoice: Your line: makes that and the action fine. The broom stays a broom; the reason changes. Day 1656, swept.
